previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a long history of chronic abdominal pain, depression, anxiety, PTSD, and hearing loss was admitted for an acute flare of her typical mid-epigastric pain and nausea. She presented with an elevated lipase of 453 but no signs of acute obstruction or gallstones on ultrasound or MRCP. Imaging showed changes consistent with chronic pancreatitis but no acute pathology. She was managed supportively with bowel rest, IV fluids, and gradual advancement from clear liquids to a soft diet. Her pain and nausea improved, and she tolerated oral intake well by discharge. All home medications, including gabapentin, imipramine, erythromycin, and hydromorphone, were continued without change. A therapist visited during admission, which the patient found helpful. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with her outpatient providers.

# Right hand cellulitis:  Secondary to IV placement, much 
improved, on IV vancomycin and cefazolin ___ has been

# Contact dermatitis:  apply steroid cream bid. Will discharge 
with Rx for steroid cream.

# Abd pain: acute on chronic. Utilized interdisciplinary care 
plan (see OMR for details).  Patient was generally very pleased 
by how the interdisciplinary plan has been working for her. Her 
abdominal pain gradually improved and her diet was slowly 
advanced.  Prior to discharge she had not received IV pain meds 
for > 2 days. Continued Tylenol, antiemetics, ranitidine, 
imipramine, home dilaudid PRN, and TID erythromycin 30 minutes 
prior to meals. On the day of discharge she was tolerating solid 
diet without vomiting or complaint of significant pain.

# IV access: IV access is extremely difficult to achieve in this 
patient, presumably due to multiple prior hospitalizations with 
IVs.  She lost access during hospitalization and the IV team was 
unable to replace the IV.  Anesthesia was called to assist with 
IV placement and they were able to place one PIV.  The patient 
subsequently lost IV access again later during hospitalization. 
Fortunately, however, at that point in her hospitalization, she 
did not require any further IV medications or IV fluids. 
However, the patient frequently requested to have an IV placed, 
""just in case I am in a lot of pain or I need IV fluids.""  At 
this point she was on oral pain medications and was tolerating 
PO.  We explained to her the difficulty of achieving IV access 
in her case and the lack of clinical indication for IV 
medications or IV fluids at that time.  She continued to persist 
in requesting IV access, despite frequent education and 
clarification about the issue, and even at one point proposed 
placing a PICC line.  She exhibited a severe lack of insight 
regarding the risks/benefits of IV access, which given that she 
is very bright, is concerning for ulterior motives.

# Reported diarrhea: patient's report of diarrhea began 
immediately upon starting oral abx for her cellulitis, which 
were discontinued after having completed a 5 day course of total 
abx and complete resolution of the cellulitis.  She is also on 
erythromycin TID w/ meals to promote bowel motility, which 
certainly could be contributing.  Also of note, she had recent 
hospital roommate who tested positive for C. diff, so that is a 
concern if her diarrhea persists despite discontinuation of abx. 
 She has no other signs/symptoms concerning for colitis.   
Diarrhea resolved since stopping abx yesterday.  She was 
tolerating a normal diet on the day of discharge without any 
diarrhea.

# PTSD, anxiety, depression: continued home prazosin, 
clonazepam, venlafaxine
